claims.statement: Tom Allen was sure Ed Smith would defeat Joe Goddard (passage garbled in OCR).
Tom Allen had picked Ed Smith to beat Joe Goddard before the fight.
Tom Allen told Ed Smith to get his head into Joe Goddard's body if he could and to stick close all the time.
Tom Allen backed Ed Smith, a Birmingham man, against Joe Goddard.
Tom Allen won heavily on his bet on Ed Smith against Joe Goddard.
Tom Allen coached Ed Smith when Smith beat Joe Goddard at the Olympic Club in New Orleans, in a fight printed as March 32, 1893.
Tom Allen was behind Ed Smith in his corner during the fight with Joe Goddard at New Orleans.
Tom Allen said Ed Smith fairly won the fight with Joe Goddard.
Tom Allen was one of Ed Smith's seconds in Smith's fight against Joe Goddard.
Tom Allen sat in a private box at the Smith-Goddard fight.
Tom Allen says Charlie Mitchell must beat Jim Corbett.
Tom Allen was stakeholder for the Sharpe-Crosby fight and held the $1,000 posted by the backers.
Tom Allen suggested the Armourdale Club postpone the fight from November 21 to the first week in December, to give Sharpe time to get in condition.
Tom Allen is confident Corbett will meet his conqueror in Charley Mitchell.
Tom Allen says Corbett's battles with Jackson and Sullivan show him to be a very ordinary fighter.
Tom Allen has secured twelve ox tails from which he will make a jelly to harden the stomach.
Tom Allen will send the jelly to Mitchell's training quarters.
Tom Allen offered Paddy Smith, brother of Denver Smith, $100 for the receipt for the jelly.
Tom Allen will have charge of preparing Mitchell's food and may be one of his seconds in the ring.
Tom Allen spent much of his time on the beach or at the top of the old Anastasia lighthouse, a stone's throw from Mitchell's cottage.
Tom Allen and Bat Masterson would like to bet $5,000 against the even-money wagers that Corbett wins in twenty rounds.
Tom Allen had prepared his famous ox-tail jelly as a stomach hardener for Charley Mitchell before the Corbett fight.
Tom Allen said he had fancied Mitchell but decided not to bet a cent on him after seeing the two men before the fight.
Tom Allen was assisting in Mitchell's training for his fight with Corbett.
Tom Allen wrote to Fred Watkins that Mitchell could not lose and was in the pink of condition.
Tom Allen wrote to Fred Watkins that he thought odds of 2 to 1 might be obtainable at the ringside.
Tom Allen wrote in a letter that Mitchell was fit to fight for a kingdom, as reported by Alderman Cronin.
Tom Allen was one of Charley Mitchell's seconds at Jacksonville.
Tom Allen is very fond of playing jokes on visitors, and in January 1894 he left a newspaper reporter waiting at Mitchell's training quarters while the trainers took a nap.
Tom Allen found a porpoise struggling in the shallow water on the beach and tried to keep it away, then reported how he had captured it to the training party.
Tom Allen was one of Charley Mitchell's seconds at the Corbett-Mitchell fight in Florida.
Tom Allen lost a diamond ring on the train home from Jacksonville, and later found it by the glitter of a piece of wire from a beer bottle.
Tom Allen said there was no fight between Corbett and Mitchell.
Tom Allen said he thoroughly believed Corbett could whip any pugilist, including Peter Jackson and Ed Smith.
Tom Allen said his ox-tail jelly hardened Mitchell's stomach all right, but Corbett punched Mitchell in the face.
Tom Allen and Tom Kelly doubt that Bob Fitzsimmons can fight successfully with his arms or wrists.
Tom Allen wrote to the Post-Dispatch that Andy Bowen's seconds should have thrown up the sponge three rounds before Bowen was knocked out by George Lavigne.
Tom Allen believed prize fighting should be held in the open air, not in enclosed arenas, and that boxing would survive the closing of the New Orleans clubs.
Tom Allen said no fight could be pulled off in any shape around St. Louis at that time, so he advised Neist to try for a wrestling match with Mooney.
Tom Allen and his old backer Fred Watkins were regular patrons of the races at the St. Louis Fair Grounds.
Tom Allen (printed as 'Tom Alle') was among the old-time pugilists missing from the Hot Springs gathering.
Tom Allen said he did not know the first principle of bull fighting but believed any so-called sport that calls for dead horses and bulls is no sport at all.
Tom Allen hung a picture of William McKinley on the wall of Champion's Rest among the best pugs and wrestlers, and backed him for president against Cleveland.
Tom Allen was in close conference with Peter Maher during the Maher and Choynski fight and had a reserved seat at the ringside.
Tom Allen said Frank Slavin's defeat by Bob Armstrong could not have ended any other way, given Slavin's condition.
Tom Allen and Tom Kelly, at the Post-Dispatch's request, watched Jim Corbett at a Havlin's Theater matinee and declared him fit to fight.
The paper describes Tom Allen as an enthusiastic Corbett man.
Tom Allen said Corbett is the fastest big man he has ever seen in the ring.
Tom Allen said Corbett would beat Fitzsimmons quickly, winding his clock before rounds were fought (headline, garbled).
Paddy Smith, brother of Denver Ed Smith, came to St. Louis and stayed with Tom Allen.
Denver Ed Smith followed his brother to St. Louis and also stayed at Tom Allen's place.
Denver Ed Smith was at Tom Allen's place in St. Louis on the morning of 1897-06-14, where he shook hands with Allen and had breakfast.
Denver Ed Smith and Ike Weir had taken up quarters at Tom Allen's place while looking for fights.
Ike Weir, the Belfast Spider, was also staying at Tom Allen's place.
Tom Allen of St. Louis offered to back Denver Ed Smith to the extent of $2,000 for a return fight with Joe Choynski or Joe Goddard, if Smith could arrange one.
Tom Allen began going to the races at the Fair Grounds in St. Louis after seeing the Derby run there on Saturday, June 26, 1897.
Tom Allen commented that Fitzsimmons was justified in his present action (the text is too garbled to read fully).
Tom Allen said Corbett should take Fitzsimmons at his word.
Allen had been drinking heavily and was still under the influence of liquor when he was moved to the Four Courts.
Tom Allen is rough and surly with most people but kind and gentle with his daughter.
